lines: ZERO needs one thing from the supermarket.
Milk.
The milk is the farthest thing from the door.
Who decided that?
Two explanations are fighting over this carton.
One has a villain.
The other has a truck.
Behind every dairy wall, there is a room like this.
Cold on purpose.
Three degrees.
For milk, cold is not a preference.
The rule says: cooled to seven degrees Celsius or less, and kept there.
So what happens when it isn’t?
One small experiment measured it.
About three hours at room temperature,
and a carton loses a whole day of shelf life.
So how does a store keep it cold, all the way from the factory?
It arrives in a refrigerated truck.
The truck backs up to a dock.
And the dock is at the back of the store.
Truck. Dock. Cold room. Dairy case.
A Wegmans manager told NPR why that matters:
“We don’t have to worry about ever breaking the cold chain.”
Now put the milk at the front door.
Every carton would cross the whole store, past the warm shelves.
Ten minutes out of the cold costs about an hour of shelf life.
So is it just plumbing?
But look at ZERO’s receipt.
He came for one thing.
He is leaving with four.
That is the other explanation: the walk-through.
Put the milk at the back, and people pass the shelves.
Some of them buy things they never planned.
But how many?
The average American supermarket carries thirty-three thousand items.
One of them has to sit farthest from the door.
And the store gets to choose which.
For decades, one number kept getting repeated.
Sixty to seventy percent of supermarket purchases are unplanned.
A 1999 study followed thirty thousand purchases in fourteen cities.
On big trips, sixty-eight percent of the items were decided in the store.
On small trips, fifty-four.
A 2008 study in Dutch supermarkets asked it another way.
For each category in the basket: planned, or decided in the store?
Eighteen percent.
About one category per trip.
Same question. Sixty-eight and eighteen.
They count different things: items against categories, American trips against Dutch ones.
Both are real. Neither is the whole story.
And do shoppers even walk past everything?
Researchers tracked thousands of carts in one supermarket.
Not one long trip went down all twelve aisles.
Most people use the outer loop as home base, and dart into the aisles they need.
So here is the whole picture.
A reason put the milk there: the truck, the cold room, the rule.
A benefit keeps it there: whoever walks to the milk passes something else.
Even the stores give both answers.
A Kroger spokesperson told NPR the cold chain, and the walk-through.
A BJ’s dairy buyer said the same: the cold chain, and “building the basket.”
A supermarket consultant told NPR the milk has been in the back for seventy to eighty years.
He would move it to the front.
In most stores, it is still back there.
What does that mean for ZERO’s basket?
In the Dutch study, shoppers who called themselves fast and efficient bought eighty-two percent less on impulse than the average shopper.
Trips for something needed right away: fifty-three percent less.
Next week, ZERO goes for milk again.
This time, he knows the way.
Some of what you buy was never on your list.
And some of what was on it never makes it home.
